title: Capturing LLM Capabilities via Evidence-Calibrated Query Clustering
claim: Surface-level semantic categories can group queries that need different capabilities, so semantic taxonomies misrepresent the latent skills a query demands.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right: queries → topics → capabilities, with a red misalignment label
description: A single rounded-border panel with three columns headed Queries, Semantic Topics and Capabilities. On the left are three colored query boxes: a gray one asking for the derivative of sin(x), an orange one asking for a proof about finite subgroups of a field's multiplicative group, and a blue one asking for a derivation of the Nernst equation. Dashed boxes in the middle column read Mathematics and Chemistry. Dashed boxes on the right read Rote Recall and Multi-step deductive derivation. Solid black arrows link query 1 to Mathematics and Mathematics to Rote Recall. A dotted orange arrow links query 2 to Mathematics, and another dotted orange arrow runs from Mathematics down to Multi-step deductive derivation. A dashed blue arrow links query 3 to Chemistry, and Chemistry then links to Multi-step deductive derivation. A bold red italic 'Misalignment!' label sits in the middle. The eye goes first to the red label and the colored arrows.
caption: Misalignment between surface-level semantics and latent capability demands.
abstract: Query clustering organizes queries into groups that reflect shared latent capability demands, enabling capability-aware LLM evaluation. Existing clustering methods, which primarily rely on semantic taxonomies or embeddings, often fail to capture such latent capability requirements due to a misalignment between surface-level semantics and actual model performance. We propose ECC, an algorithm that calibrates prior semantic embeddings using limited posterior model comparisons to bridge the gap between surface-level semantics and latent capability requirements. ECC characterizes each cluster through a capability profile parameterized by a Bradley-Terry model and uses trainable mixture weights to accommodate queries with mixed capability demands, jointly learning a flexible, capability-aware clustering structure that supports query-specific inference of LLM capabilities. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that ECC significantly improves LLM capability ranking quality, outperforming human-labeled and embedding-based baselines by an average of 17.64 and 18.02 percentage points, respectively, and proves effective in downstream tasks such as query routing.
